content.text:
A walk is often recommended as a cure for an unproductive afternoon, but its benefits are easy to overstate. Walking will not supply a missing fact or remove every difficult decision. What it can do is alter the conditions in which a problem is considered. A change of pace and scenery may loosen attention without dispersing it completely.

That distinction matters. People sometimes return from a walk pleased by a stream of ideas, only to discover that most are variations on the first thought they had. The value of the walk is not the number of ideas produced. It is the chance to notice which idea survives when the mind is no longer pushing it forward.

For this reason, a walk works best as a transition rather than an escape. A short route between two deliberate periods of work can create enough distance for judgement, while a long stroll used to postpone an unpleasant task merely gives postponement a pleasant appearance.

questions.prompt: What qualification does the writer make about walks in the first paragraph?

options.text: They are effective only in unfamiliar places.
They do not solve problems by supplying missing information.
They make difficult decisions disappear.
They require a complete break from attention.

questions.explanation: The writer says a walk cannot supply a missing fact or remove every decision.

questions.prompt: According to the second paragraph, what is more important than the number of ideas?

options.text: whether an idea remains convincing afterwards
whether other people approve of them
how quickly they are recorded
how unusual they initially seem

questions.explanation: The writer values the ideas that survive after the mind stops actively pushing them.

questions.prompt: The writer mentions ‘variations on the first thought’ to suggest that

options.text: walking always produces repetitive thinking
initial enthusiasm can make ideas seem more original than they are
people should avoid reflecting while walking
creative work requires other people’s suggestions

questions.explanation: A stream of ideas may feel productive even when it merely repeats the first one.

questions.prompt: What does the writer recommend a walk should be?

options.text: an unplanned replacement for work
a transition between focused work periods
a long activity undertaken at the end of the day
an opportunity to avoid judgement

questions.explanation: The final paragraph calls it a transition and describes a short route between work periods.

questions.prompt: What is meant by ‘postponement a pleasant appearance’?

options.text: A delay can feel acceptable simply because it is enjoyable.
A walk makes an unpleasant task easier to complete.
Pleasure prevents people from delaying decisions.
A task becomes more attractive after exercise.

questions.explanation: The phrase warns that an enjoyable walk can disguise avoidance as a sensible activity.

questions.prompt: Which best describes the writer’s approach?

options.text: balanced and analytical
mocking and dismissive
enthusiastic but uncritical
uncertain and contradictory

questions.explanation: The writer identifies genuine benefits but carefully limits the claims made for walking.
